The course is intended for students with a background of DSE Physics and basic calculus. There are some overlap with DSE Physics curriculum, with come calculus mixed in. Two major topics are covered: basic Newtonian mechanics and thermodynamics. Although the course says "with Calculus," the only calculus you need is basic one variable derivatives and integrals, and most of the content does not need any calculus to answer as derivations are not tested.

- Motions and Newton's laws
- Work and energy
- Conservation of energy and momentum
- Rotation
- Rigid body
- Simple harmonic and damped oscillations
- Forced oscillations
- Standing waves and sound waves
- Kinetic theory
- The laws of thermodynamics

comment_content:
Lecture:
lecture 1-7 covers secondary-school-level content of motion, mechanical energy and momentum&impulse. There are some extensions, which are managable if you learned physics well in secondary school. 
lecture 8-11 covers the dynamics of rigid bodies. There is a short review of secondary-school-level rotational motion, with new concepts such as moment of inertia, torque, angular momentum. The lecture 11, where gyroscope is demostrated and explained, is not imprortant but extremely difficult to understand.
Lecture 12-13 covers gravitation. Some of the content is taught in secondary school with some extensions such as black hole.
Lecture 14-17 covers periodic motion and wave. The content ranges from secondary-school-level to more difficult concepts and formulas, which can be confusing for students to differentiate.   
Lecture 18-24 covers thermodynamics. Almost everything is new except equation of state. The formulas are not overly difficult, but you need to thoroughly understand the concepts and how the formulas are derived, as some exam questions may be related to these.
Tutorial:
The tutorial sessions are meant for reviewing and practicing the content covered in the lectures. Please note that attendance is taken for the tutorials by having students hand in a practice paper provided in class. Once you submit the practice paper, which usually contains 2 longer questions, your attendance will be recorded regardless of your performance on that paper.
After completing the practice paper, the TA will briefly explain the quetions and talk about 1 or 2 supplementary questions. Sometimes the TA can provide some practical methods that were not covered in the lectures. However, the tutorial sessions can be boring most of the time.
Remark: Textbook is compulsory is this course, otherwise students can't have the access code for homework.

comment_grading:
Tutorials         5%
Assignments 10%
Midterm      35%
Final Exam   50%
For the tutorials, students can earn the the mark simply by attending the assigned tutorial session. Attendance may not be recorded if you attend a tutorial session that you did not officially enroll in. Except for the two tutorial sessions that do not count towards the course grade, students are allowed to be absent for a maximum of 2 tutorial sessions without losing any tutorial grade.
For the assignments, there are a total of 11 homework assignments that count towards the course grade. Each assignment contains around 12 questions, with several parts to each question. Students are allowed a maximum of 6 attempts per question. Failure on MC question attempts will lead to a loss of grade, but students can attain full marks on calculation-based questions as long as they figure them out within the 6 attempts.There is also a dynamic study module for each chapter. Students can earn bonus points as compensation for their homework performance. After adding up the bonus points, the best 9 homework sets will be counted towards the final homework grade, meaning the lowest 2 sets will be dropped. Collaboration with classmates is recommended to ensure students can earn the maximum marks on the homework assignments.
The midterm exam covers content from Lectures 1-11. The mean score for the midterm was 15.5 out of 28, with a standard deviation of 5.6. The midterm consists of 28 MCs, all weighted equally. The majority of the questions require calculations using the formulas taught in the course. An interesting observation is that the midterm for this course seems to frequently conflict with midterms for other courses that many students take concurrently. For example, in the Fall 2023-2024 semester, the PHYS1112 midterm was scheduled on the same day as the COMP1021 midterm. This semester, the PHYS1112 midterm was scheduled on the same day as the MATH1014 midterm, creating a challenging weekend for students.
The final is comprehensive with 3/4 of the questions selected from the content covered in lecture 12-24. The mean is 22.5 out of 40 and the SD is 7.51.The final exam consists of 40 MCs, all weighted equally. Similar to the midterm, the majority of the questions require calculations using the formulas taught in the course. However, some questions also test the students' understanding of the conceptual derivation of the formulas and concepts. Therefore, in addition to remembering all the relevant formulas, students must also be familiar with the underlying conceptual development and derivation of the formulas covered throughout the course.
comment_workload: The high workload is a significant challenge in this course. Students are required to complete a set of weekly homework assignments, which typically take 2-3 hours to finish individually. After completing the homework, students may need to spend additional time on adaptive follow-up assignments if they score below 95% on the original homework. In addition to the homework, there is a set of supplementary questions that are similar in nature to the homework set. These supplementary questions typically require around 2 hours to complete.The dynamic study modules are relatively easier and usually take around 20 minutes to complete each set. Beyond the regular assignments, students may need to invest significant time in other learning activities to fully understand the course concepts. This can include reading the textbook, searching for explanations online, watching recordings of lectures by other instructors, and seeking clarification from TA, it's time-consuming.

comment_content:
Having completed PHYS 111, I feel equipped to offer a mixed but ultimately positive review of this foundational course. As a student who entered with only a high school physics background, I found the course to be a significant but manageable step up in difficulty. The initial description was a bit confusing to decipher, mentioning pathways for both beginners and advanced students, but in practice, the course does a solid job of building from the ground up for those willing to put in the work.
The heart of the course lies in its learning outcomes. We spent a substantial amount of time mastering the use of Newton's laws to solve complex, single-body dynamics problems, which forms the bedrock of classical mechanics. The modules on conservation of energy and momentum were particularly enlightening, providing powerful tools to predict outcomes in collisions and rotational motion without getting bogged down in complex forces. The latter part of the semester, covering waves and thermodynamics, was challenging but rewarding. Learning to explain phenomena like interference, the Doppler effect, and applying the laws of thermodynamics to real-world problems genuinely changed how I see the physical world.
The prescribed textbook, University Physics by Pearson, was an indispensable resource. The lectures were crucial for understanding the concepts, but the textbook problems and examples were where the real learning happened for me. I do, however, have some critiques. Some of the learning outcome phrasing, like "use solenius language," seems to be a typo (likely meaning "scientific language"), which caused minor confusion. Furthermore, the "Review Feedback" section with HKD figures is completely irrelevant and should be removed, as it adds unnecessary clutter.
Overall, PHYS 111 is a demanding course that requires consistent effort. The mathematical prerequisite is no joke; you need to be comfortable with calculus to keep up. But for students seeking a rigorous introduction to university-level physics that successfully teaches you to analyze and solve problems systematically, this course is an excellent choice. It’s tough, but you’ll come out the other side with a much stronger understanding of how the world works.

comment_content:
The course covers classical mechanics very systematically and is quite comprehensive for an introductory university physics course.
Main topics covered (roughly in order):
- Kinematics (1D & 2D), forces, Newton's laws
- Friction, inclined planes, circular motion (uniform & non-uniform)
- Work, kinetic energy, potential energy, power, conservative/non-conservative forces
- Momentum, impulse, collisions (elastic & inelastic), center of mass
- Rotational kinematics, torque, moment of inertia, rotational energy
- Rolling motion, angular momentum conservation
- Gravitation (basic), simple harmonic motion (brief introduction in some years)
comment_teaching:
Teaching quality varies quite significantly depending on the professor and TA team.
Some professors focus heavily on conceptual understanding + derivation, blackboard teaching is clear but pace can be fast
Some rely very much on PowerPoint + many worked examples, but explanations sometimes feel rushed when concepts are difficult
My Professor have a "special" english pronunciation. So good luck! 
Tutorials usually the most helpful part of the course. Good TAs can make a huge difference.  
Many students rely on tutorial notes + tutorial question bank more than lecture notes.

Lectures are dense, so it helps to read ahead or review right after class. Overall, teaching is solid but requires students to put in extra effort outside lectures.
comment_grading: Grading is typically exam-heavy. Midterms and finals carry significant weight, with smaller portions from assignments and quizzes. Exams are not only about memorization but test problem-solving skills, often requiring multiple steps. Curve adjustment is usually applied, which can balance the difficulty.
comment_workload: Moderate to heavy. Weekly assignments take time if you want to understand the problems thoroughly. Tutorials and labs add to the workload but are useful for clarifying concepts. Consistent effort throughout the semester is necessary; cramming at the end is not effective for this course.

comment_content:
This physics course goes much beyond 1112. It really focuses on why each physics quantity came to be and how everything is derived. E.g. instead of simply introducing momentum as mass times velocity, this content really focuses why mass times velocity was considered as a relevant quantity in the study of physics, why the sum of momentum of a system is more useful than the sum of its velocities etc. If you plan on doing a physics major, I highly recommend taking this course. Otherwise maybe don't (unless you really like physics).
That being said, none of the lecture material is really relevant in solving hw and exam problems. You could just read the standard 1112 lecture notes and be fine, as far as knowledge is concerned. Of course the problems are significantly more challenging that 1112 questions but they don't really utilise any of the content from the lecture notes of 1312. Thus, there is really a dissonance between what's taught in classes and what's assessed. 
The lectures and problems makes heavy use of vectors and calculus (even as far as multivariable calculus) and especially their relevance in physics. The mathematics used in the course doesn't feel like a copout. Often times when calculus-based questions are set in physics question, it ends up just being a math question without needing much physics (e.g. find the distance travelled when a velocity function is given; this question doesn't really test much physics knowledge but tests your integration skills). However, in this course, the calculus is never the focus of the questions even if you need to use it. All problems solved in lectures, hw and exams feel like physics questions and not just math questions.
TLDR; the lecture content goes into a lot depth about the origins and relevance of concepts in mechanics but the lecture content is very irrelevant to hw and exams. Take this course if you plan on doing a physics major, otherwise don't. Also don't take this course if you don't understand mathematics conceptually.

comment_content:
The lecture provided a comprehensive overview that encompassed the detailed introduction to the intricate risk management process. It delved into not only the fundamental concepts but also explored the diverse range of risks that exist within companies and society at large. Notably, the content leaned more towards the theoretical aspects, laying a solid foundation in concepts and principles rather than emphasizing complex quantitative calculations. 
On the other hand, the tutorial sessions were highly practical. They focused on equipping students with the skills to calculate Value at Risk (VaR) using the powerful tool of Excel. This involved learning various functions and techniques, along with the application of what-if analysis to understand the potential impacts of different scenarios. It was indeed a challenging learning experience, but simultaneously, it managed to spark the interest of many students due to its hands-on nature. 
For first-year students who lacked any prior business background, the overall content could prove to be quite arduous. The concepts and techniques were new and often required a significant amount of effort to grasp. However, given that it was part of the common core curriculum, the pressure to achieve a perfect understanding was somewhat alleviated. 
Nevertheless, for those in the CCC program, this particular course might not be the most advisable choice. The reason being that the examination format was rather demanding. It required students to write out their answers by hand in a closed-book setting. This placed a heavy emphasis on rote learning and the ability to recall information accurately. In contrast, if the exam were to be an open-book format, it would transform into a course where students could potentially achieve excellent grades, as they would have the freedom to refer to relevant materials and focus more on applying their knowledge rather than simply memorizing it.
